body.text: Since August, the Myanmar regime led by Min Aung Hlaing has intensified a series of economic measures that at first glance appear to be unrelated. They have increased restrictions on border trade and the overseas use of Myanmar-based mobile payment services. They have tightened passport procedures for citizens abroad and intensified efforts to compel migrant workers to use the state-controlled financial system for remittances. They have also increased efforts to attract foreign direct investment (FDI).

We argue that these efforts show that the regime is doubling down on a strategy of economic control. However, these measures are not likely to address the drivers of Myanmar’s foreign exchange and economic challenges.

One pillar of the regime’s strategy is restricting cross-border imports entering Myanmar, to cut off revenues from anti-regime groups and curb foreign exchange outflows. Border trade is an important way for Myanmar’s people to access essential goods and is also important for China and Thailand, Myanmar’s main border trade partners. Yet trade along the Myanmar-China border and at Tachilek on the Myanmar-Thailand border has faced heavy restrictions. The number of large trucks permitted to ply the route has been severely limited. Goods now come across in smaller vehicles or on foot, with individuals limited to two bags per crossing. At Myawaddy, Myanmar’s busiest border crossing with Thailand, the regime-allied Border Guard Force has also restricted truck movements, which pushes trade through informal channels while raising consumer prices for scarce imports.

Another pillar of the strategy is trying to increase control of foreign exchange inflows. Myanmar mobile payment services, including KBZPay, Wave Money, AYA Pay and CB Pay, have reportedly faced new restrictions on overseas use. Migrant workers and their families use these services to transfer money outside official banking channels because they offer better exchange rates, allowing recipients to get more kyats for the same amount of foreign exchange. The restrictions aim to regulate digital payments and can be seen as part of a broader effort to prevent foreign exchange from bypassing the regime-controlled financial system.

The regime is applying similar controls on migrant remittances, a key source of foreign exchange. In August, the authorities promoted the Family Remittance Management System, in collaboration with the Central Bank of Myanmar, relevant banks and licensed overseas employment agencies. This system will monitor migrant workers to ensure they remit 25 per cent of their salaries through official channels. Migrants are facing further pressure as embassies in Bangkok, Singapore and Australia suspend or delay passport services, forcing some applicants to seek clearance from Naypyidaw or return to Myanmar to renew their passports. These measures extend the regime’s oversight of citizens abroad, forcing them to send at least some foreign currency remittances back through state-controlled banks.

The regime’s logic is not hard to discern. Several border crossings and trade routes are held by anti-regime armed groups, so restricting cross-border flows denies them revenue and supplies. The regime needs more forex, partly for conflict-related purposes. However, inflows through the state-controlled system are declining due to the regime’s policies, which misprice forex: the migrant worker remittance rate and official rate are overvalued by 20 and 120 per cent, respectively. This discourages sales through official channels. Instead of reforming exchange rate policies to address these changes, the regime has compressed imports through licensing restrictions and border closures, and previously tried restricting import licenses and closing borders. However, these measures only temporarily relieved forex challenges.

While controls can conserve foreign exchange, they cannot generate it. Instead, they undermine economic activities that can generate foreign exchange. For example, Myanmar’s garment industry depends on imports for 95 per cent of inputs, including fabrics and buttons, to produce goods for export. Restricting access to these inputs makes it harder for factories to maintain production, thereby reducing exports and, in turn, foreign exchange inflows. Similarly, the controls hurt construction companies dependent on imported building materials. Overall, the controls cause supply disruptions that raise costs, delay production, and sometimes force businesses to suspend operations, thus hurting foreign exchange inflows.
The regime’s import and exchange rate controls distort incentives, push trade and financial transactions towards informal channels and deter investment.

Min Aung Hlaing’s diplomatic strategy in 2026 has also focused on attracting investment. Bringing along Myanmar business leaders on his visits to India, China, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Russia and Belarus, he promoted investment in agriculture, energy, mining and infrastructure, including the Dawei Special Economic Zone and Yadanabon Cyber City. He has also sought Russian cooperation on nuclear power and space technology. Though these trips are often interpreted through the lens of diplomatic recognition, they reflect Myanmar’s urgent need for new foreign capital.

Min Aung Hlaing’s attempts to woo foreign capital are partly undermined by his regime’s policies. Investors need confidence that they can repatriate their initial capital and profits, and that they can transfer funds into the country at exchange rates that reflect market conditions and make operations viable, but current policies restrict this, undermining investor confidence. Frequent changes in rules and regulations also affect investor confidence. Over time, the regime’s controls may weaken the formal economy and reduce the country’s capacity to generate foreign exchange.

The regime’s efforts to exert more control via import and exchange policies, while restricting forex outflows and seeking new investment, will thus face challenges. The current import and exchange rate controls distort incentives, push trade and financial transactions towards informal channels and deter investment. These controls consolidate foreign exchange with the state while creating a forex shortage for businesses and ordinary citizens. Shifting costs onto the public cannot build long-term economic stability.
